newsitem.title: USA: King World, Sony in legal dispute.
newsitem.headline: King World, Sony in legal dispute.

text.p: King World Productions Inc., which distributes such popular television game shows as "Wheel of Fortune" and "Jeopardy!", wants to get into the more lucrative part of the business -- production.

The New York-based syndication giant recently asked a U.S. Court to decide if an existing game show distribution agreement with Sony Corp. precludes King World from producing other game shows on its own.
Sony, which produces "Wheel of Fortune" and "Jeopardy!", filed a response last week seeking unspecified damages from King World, which it said breached its distribution contract.

On Tuesday, King World fired back, calling the Sony suit without merit and pledging to aggressively litigate the matter. King World maintains it still has the right to produce game shows, provided the distribution is handled by another party.

King World was not immediately available for comment but a source close to the company said it decided to seek a legal resolution at this time because it is interested in producing a new edition of "Hollywood Squares," the question-and-answer show featuring Hollywood celebrities which was a longstanding hit during the 1970s.
He added that because its contracts with Sony are so lucrative, King World "wasn't just going to go ahead and begin producing Hollywood Squares" without a ruling that it had the legal right to do so.

News of the litigation was disclosed in a filing King World made with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The company said it filed an action on March 24 in California Superior Court seeking to confirm its rights to produce strip game shows, or those that run five days a week.
"King World has never taken any action that would breach the agreements under which it distrubutes 'Wheel of Fortune' and 'Jeopardy!', Chairman Roger King said in a statement.'"

Indeed, King World has, in recent months, succeeded in licensing "Wheel of Fortune" and "Jeopardy!" through the 2001-2002 television season in markets covering more than 75 percent of the United States.
Sony was not immediately available to respond.
By voicing an interest in expanding into the game show production business, King World is confirming the speculation of many people in the industry.

While the two Sony game shows, as well as "The Oprah Winfrey Show," which King World also distributes, are some of the most successful shows in syndication, there is also concern those shows are past their prime. More recently launched shows, like the news magazine "American Journal," have not showed as much promise. In addition, there has been conjecture about how King World will spend a large store of cash it has on hand.
"King World certainly wants to be in the production and the distribution business," the King World Source said.
Still, some analysts downplayed the significance of the outcome of the Sony lawsuit.

"It's significant but it's not earth-shaking for the future of the company," said Cowen & Co. analyst Harold Vogel. Were the court to rule against King World, he said they would still be left with the rights to produce talk shows, or other non-game show formats.
